sources.note: No descriptive references at all (Glottolog lists no grammar, sketch or phonology); only the ISO change request and the Grierson recordings entry; alt names Wewau, Wewaw; status extinct.

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 code page for wea; Wikidata Q15895870
ISO 639-3 Registration Authority (2011). Change Request 2011-078: merge Wewaw [wea] into Sgaw Karen [ksw] (rejected 2012-02-03). Submitted by the Ethnologue editor, SIL International. 5 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on phonology or stress. States (p. 2): 'There is only very old and sketchy evidence that Wewaw as a language has ever existed. The only data (a wordlist and a recording of the Prodigal Son story) comes from the Linguistic Survey of India (1920s) and the latest referent is in the 1921 Census of Burma which lists 256 speakers'; 'If it still exists, it is the name of a divergent dialect of Sgaw Karen [ksw].' Sources it cites: Census of Burma 1911/1931; Saw Hser Gay 2009 thesis (Karen Baptist Theological Seminary); dsal LSI Burma recordings; Bradley 1997.

sources.citation: Bradley, David (1997). Tibeto-Burman languages and classification. In D. Bradley (ed.), Papers in Southeast Asian Linguistics No. 14: Tibeto-Burman Languages of the Himalayas, 1-72. Pacific Linguistics A-86.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Cited in the ISO CR for Karenic classification; would at most place Wewaw within Sgaw; no phonology expected. Open PDF not reached by automated download (SEAlang/ANU mirrors did not respond).

sources.citation: Grierson, George A. (ed.) (1928). Linguistic Survey of India. Vol. I, Part II: Comparative Vocabulary. Calcutta: Government of India Central Publication Branch. [Introduction 'Karen languages' pp. 14-18; Wewaw = language no. 41a throughout the vocabulary; list supplied by L. F. Taylor, collected 'on the borders of the Toungoo and Karenni districts']
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Only primary written Wewaw data ever published: the standard LSI list in Roman transcription with aspiration marks but NO tone or stress marks. Grierson, Introduction p. 14 (scanned-corrected): 'These remarks apply only to the literary forms of Pwo and Sga, for which alone have I been able to find words written in the Karen Alphabet, with the tones marked throughout. For the other Karen dialects I have been confined to lists in the Roman character, in which no attempt has been made to mark the Tones.' P. 17: Taylor's lists 'include those for.. Bwe, Wewaw, Karenbyu..'; 'the Wewaw list on the b…

sources.citation: Grierson, George A. (1927). Linguistic Survey of India, Vol. I Part I: Introductory. Calcutta: Government of India Central Publication Branch.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on Wewaw phonology. Chapter III 'Karen and Man' says the Karen family is 'Neither.. described in the pages of the present Survey' and 'I must leave to the Linguistic Survey of Burma the task of describing the various forms of Karen'. Wewaw appears only in Appendix II (gramophone record list: '41a. Wewaw, Burma, 5518-AK') and in the language index ('Wewa or Wewaw.. 256' speakers).

sources.citation: Grantham, S. G. (1923). Census of India 1921, Vol. X: Burma, Part I Report. Rangoon: Government Printing. Appendix B (Karen languages).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on phonology. Classifies Karen dialects into groups: 'Group I: Sgaw, Paku, Wewaw and probably Monnepwa'; subsidiary table lists 'N4. Wewaw.. 250' speakers, in Toungoo/Yamethin districts.

sources.citation: Linguistic Survey of India gramophone records, Burma set (Grierson 1920-1929 'Linguistic Survey of Burma' = Glottolog ref 94361): record 5518-AK, 'Karen, Sgaw dialect, Wewaw or Wewa form', Parable of the prodigal son. Digital South Asia Library, University of Chicago.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Audio only (c. 3 min, monaural mp3). The DSAL database record has empty narrator/location/transcription fields; there is no written description or transcription. This is the only primary language data for Wewaw that could be located.

sources.citation: Spearman, H. R. (ed.) (1879). The British Burma Gazetteer. Vol. II [alphabetical]. Rangoon: Government Press. s.v. 'We-wa' (p. 853); s.v. 'Sgaw'; s.v. 'Bghai-ka-hta' (p. 121). [Karen entries from Francis Mason's JASB papers]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No phonology content; ethnographic entry; only linguistic remark is that the dialect is 'a mixture of Sgaw and Bghai'.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Wewaw language' (redirects into the S'gaw Karen article, which lists Wewaw among divergent S'gaw dialects alongside Paku, Mopwa, Monnepwa)
sources.note: Nothing specific to Wewaw; only general S'gaw Karen phonology.

sources.citation: Linguistic Survey of Burma (Grierson, ed., 1917-1920s): the unpublished Wewaw wordlist and the manuscript specimen (transcription/translation) that accompanied gramophone record 5518-AK. The ISO CR 2011-078 says 'a wordlist and a recording of the Prodigal Son story' are the only data.
